stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Maren Oyelaran's 2011 novel The Tide Tables. Ines, a graduate student in marine biology, is surveying tide pools with her adviser, Dr. Achebe.

Ines had long assumed that fieldwork would be the dull part of her training: hours of crouching over tide pools and tallying sea stars on a clipboard while her real thinking waited back at the lab. Yet by the third morning she no longer noticed the cold water soaking her knees. She had begun to know each pool by its residents: the one with the orange star missing an arm, the one where a hermit crab kept reclaiming the same shell. When Dr. Achebe called out that the tide was turning, Ines looked up, startled, as if woken from sleep.
choices: To show Dr. Achebe's satisfaction with the progress Ines is making as a researcher
To portray a character's growing absorption in work she had expected to find tedious
To describe the specific methods Ines used to count the sea stars in each pool
To convey Ines's frustration that fieldwork was keeping her away from the lab
explanation: The setup line tells you Ines is the focus. The text opens with what she 'had long assumed': that fieldwork would be dull. After 'Yet', it shows that belief being overturned. She stops noticing the cold, she knows each pool by its residents, and she is startled when she's pulled out of her concentration. Put simply, the excerpt shows her becoming absorbed in work she expected to be tedious, which is what this choice says.

A.why: You moved the focus to the wrong person. Dr. Achebe only calls out that the tide is turning. The text never shows any satisfaction on the adviser's part. The excerpt is about Ines's experience.

C.why: You picked a concrete detail the text never gives. It mentions tallying on a clipboard but explains no counting method. The details it does give, like the one-armed star and the hermit crab, show how absorbed Ines has become, not how she counts.

D.why: You stopped at the first sentence. Ines expected fieldwork to be dull, but after 'Yet' the text shows that expectation was wrong. She loses track of time in the pools and is not frustrated to be away from the lab.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Tomas Relwyn's 1998 poem "To a Student on Her First Dig." The speaker addresses a young archaeologist.

You will kneel for days and find nothing: / only soil, a root, the brown sameness of the trench. / Some will tell you this is wasted time. / But the earth gives up its cups and coins / only to hands that have learned its slowness. / Keep brushing. The shard that waits for you / has waited a thousand years already; / it is in no hurry, and neither, now, are you.
choices: To warn a young archaeologist that most excavations yield nothing of lasting value
To lament the many years the speaker spent searching for artifacts without success
To describe the particular objects the speaker once uncovered at an excavation site
To encourage a young archaeologist to keep working patiently through fruitless days
explanation: The poem is addressed to 'you', the young archaeologist. It admits the dull days are coming, then turns at 'But': the earth rewards hands that have 'learned its slowness'. The command 'Keep brushing' and the promise that a shard 'waits for you' are encouraging. The poem urges the student to be patient and keep going.

A.why: You reversed the tone. The poem does say there will be days of finding nothing, but it treats them as the price of eventual discovery. It promises a find ('the shard that waits for you'). That is encouragement, not a warning.

B.why: You moved the focus from the addressee to the speaker. The poem is about the student ('You will kneel', 'Keep brushing') and says nothing about the speaker's own years of searching. It does not lament anything.

C.why: You treated a general image as a specific detail. 'Cups and coins' stand for what the earth yields to patient diggers in general. The poem never describes objects the speaker actually found at any site.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Priya Ramaswamy's 2016 memoir Low Water. The narrator's father worked for a regional water agency in the 1970s.

Every morning at six, my father drove to the gauging station on the Senna and wrote down a single number: the height of the river. As a child I could not understand why anyone would do this. The river looked the same to me each day, brown and slow. Only years later, reading his ledgers after he died, did I see what he had seen. The numbers rose and fell like breathing; they held every drought and every flood of my childhood, recorded in his careful hand before any of us knew what they meant.
choices: To convey the narrator's belated understanding of why a parent's daily task mattered
To portray the father's pride in the accuracy of the river measurements he recorded
To explain the procedure the gauging station used to measure the river each morning
To show the narrator's lasting resentment of the early hours the father spent at work
explanation: The focus is the narrator. It is the narrator who 'could not understand' the father's routine as a child, and who 'Only years later' sees its meaning. The ledgers turn out to hold every drought and flood. In plain words, the excerpt shows the narrator coming to understand, late, why the father's daily routine mattered.

B.why: You moved the focus to the wrong person. The father appears in the text, but it never describes his feelings about his work. The excerpt is about how the narrator's understanding changed over time.

C.why: You picked a detail the text never gives. It says the father 'wrote down a single number' but never explains how the station measured the river. The excerpt is about what those numbers came to mean to the narrator.

D.why: You misread both the feeling and how long it lasted. As a child the narrator was puzzled, not resentful. And the puzzlement did not last: reading the ledgers later, the narrator 'did see what he had seen.'

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Hal Dorsey's 2004 novel The Listening Year. Wen, a linguist, is recording an elderly speaker in a remote mountain valley.

Wen adjusted the microphone and asked Mrs. Oshana for the word for 'first snow.' The old woman answered with a sound Wen had never heard, a soft click folded into a vowel, and Wen felt the thrill every field linguist waits years for. She wrote it down carefully. Then Mrs. Oshana added that her grandson did not know the word, nor did anyone else still living in the valley, and the thrill in Wen's chest turned heavy. She had found something new, she realized, only because it was nearly gone.
choices: To portray Mrs. Oshana's regret that her grandson never learned the valley's language
To explain how Wen transcribed the unfamiliar click sound in her field notebook
To portray a linguist's mixed feelings on recording a word that is nearly lost
To convey Wen's confidence that the valley's language can still be fully revived
explanation: The setup line makes Wen the focus. The excerpt first shows her 'thrill' at hearing a new sound. Then, at 'Then', it shows that thrill turning 'heavy' when she learns no one else knows the word. The last sentence joins the two feelings: she found something new only because it was nearly gone. Your plain-words summary should be that she is torn between excitement and sorrow.

A.why: You moved the focus to the wrong person. Mrs. Oshana reports that her grandson doesn't know the word, but the text never describes how she feels about it. The feelings the excerpt traces belong to Wen.

B.why: You picked a detail the text never gives. It says only that Wen 'wrote it down carefully' and never explains how she transcribed the click. That moment is part of the setup, not the point of the excerpt.

D.why: You reversed the emotional direction. Wen's thrill 'turned heavy' when she realized the word was 'nearly gone.' Nothing in the text suggests she is confident the language can be revived.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Clara Venn's 1987 novel The Far Side of August. The narrator, a twelve-year-old girl, is using her uncle's telescope for the first time.

I had always believed that a telescope would make the stars enormous, like the glossy photographs in Uncle Ruben's books. But when I pressed my eye to the eyepiece, Saturn was tiny, no bigger than a grain of rice, and pale. For a moment I nearly said I was disappointed. Then I noticed the ring, a thin line of light standing clear of the planet, and understood that I was not looking at a picture. I was looking at the thing itself, across all that dark, and it was there.
choices: To portray Uncle Ruben's delight at sharing his telescope with his young relative
To convey the narrator's wonder at seeing a planet directly despite its small image
To describe the narrator's disappointment that the telescope showed so little detail
To explain why telescopes show planets as smaller than photographs in books do
explanation: The text sets up what the narrator 'had always believed', that Saturn would look enormous. After 'But', it shows her expectation let down. Then it turns again: seeing the ring, she realizes she is looking at 'the thing itself.' Taken as a whole, the excerpt shows her disappointment giving way to wonder at seeing a real planet directly, however small it looks.

A.why: You moved the focus to the wrong person. Uncle Ruben is mentioned only as the owner of the books and the telescope. The text never shows how he feels. The excerpt is about the narrator's reaction.

C.why: You stopped halfway. The narrator 'nearly said' she was disappointed, but she didn't. Noticing the ring changed her reaction, and the excerpt ends in wonder, not disappointment.

D.why: You credited the text with an explanation it never gives. It notes that Saturn looked smaller than in the photographs but never says why. The excerpt is about the narrator's feelings, not about optics.
